AW-STUDY-0049

Paint the World

A card you play. Paint falls out of the sky onto the board, stays for one day of in-game time, and strange plants grow out of it. It is Splatoon's idea that the paint is the play, turned into something gentle: you do not fight over the ground, you make a garden of it.

Day 1 · 09:00

Play the card, then press +6 hours a few times (or leave it running: a game day is three minutes). Sprouts show up in the first hours, the plants grow through the morning and open by evening. At the end of the day the paint dries and shrinks away. The plants stay a few more days, then sink back into the soil.

The idea in one picture

1. Play the card

One card in the hand, tapped like the tile cards. It picks two bold colours from five and rains four splats around where you are looking.

2. Paint falls

Teardrops stretch as they fall, hit the ground and spread with a little overshoot, flinging droplets. The ground sings a soft plop (the sound is the Ranch's own, no new engine).

3. A day of colour

Wet and glossy for the first hours, then chalky, then it shrinks away over the last quarter of the day. At night it glows softly, so a painted board is a lantern board.

4. Plants grow

Each colour grows its own species. Sprout, grow, bloom over about twenty game hours. A different colour grows a different plant, so the player learns the colours by growing them.

What we took from Splatoon, and what we left

Style: yes

  • The paint is the game: the shader is the verb, not a skin.
  • Two bold colours on a calm, quiet world, so the paint always reads. The Ranch is soft green, which is a good canvas.
  • Glossy wet look, wobbly outline, flung droplets, a splat that overshoots then settles. Kids read it as "fresh paint" instantly.

Expression: never

  • No squid or Inkling forms, no weapons, no team turf score, no shooter moves.
  • No Nintendo art, names, sounds or colours copied. The splat shapes come from our own seeded recipe.
  • Nothing here is a fight. A friend can play it too and the board just gets prettier.

From the Oracle

Splatoon 3's record says "paint the world as the score" and "hide a model swap behind a splash". We use the second one for the plants: a sprout never pops in, it rises through its own paint. The score idea stays out for now, because the Ranch is a place, not a match.

How it shows information (the HUD grammar)

Diegetic

The paint is in the world and the people and animals know it: sheep wander through it, bots can react to a bright field. Colour tells you the plant to expect.

Overlay: one thing only

The card in the hand. There is no timer bar. The age of the paint is simply how dry it looks, and how big the plants are.

The whole game adapts

The same day clock drives light, night glow, plant size and the paint fading. Watercolour distance (AW-STUDY-0045 #6) composes: far paint softens its edges and turns pastel, like the far hills.

The rules, plainly

ThingRule
Paint life24 in-game hours from landing. Wet glint for 4 hours, dries, shrinks over the last 6.
Plant startUnder two hours after landing, so they sprout one by one.
Plant stagesSprout 0 to 4 h, grow 4 to 8 h, bloom 8 to 12 h after the plant starts. It stays in bloom, swaying and glowing at night.
Plant life72 hours, then it sinks back into the soil over 4 hours.
ClockEverything derives from the game day clock (day * 24 + hour). Pause stops it; changing the time of day moves it. There are no timers.
Splat ballsSpending the card gives a random handful: 3 to 7 balls (five is the usual) at a random size from tiny (.55x) to giant (1.6x). Drag a ball from the right edge and let go; the flick carries it, it lands, splats and grows plants. Bigger splats grow more plants.
Caps14 splats, 30 plants, oldest returns first. A card is 4 splats.
Where it playsThe Sandbox tile board today, and any board that gives the module a scene, a height function and the clock (the Winchester dioramas are next).
KidsPG, no violence. Paint never covers people or animals; it is only on the ground.

Performance, held to the tile-placement standard

No shader compiles on play

One splat shader and one plant material are compiled when the board loads (warm()). Playing a card compiles nothing.

No scene rebuilds

The paint lives on a pool of fourteen pre-made draped meshes; a play rewrites one position buffer per splat. Nothing about a tile changes, and no tile material is touched.

Few draws

A plant is three meshes (stalk, head, glow). Thirty plants and fourteen splats is about 100 draw calls and under 25,000 triangles at the most.

Tour and what comes next

tour: yes

It is a card and a verb a new player can do in one tap, with a payoff within minutes. It goes in the player tour as "Play the Paint card and watch what grows." Evan can drop it from the tour by flipping tour to false in whats-new.json.

Next: the plants as ingredients (the café's menu), the paint as footprints for the dog, and a second card colour pair in the Moonbase dialect (lights, not paint).

Five low-poly plants, one per paint colour. Each is built from named parts, flat shaded, with three growth stages you can scrub. Drag to orbit, scroll or pinch to zoom.

The card

Paint the World

Cards v3 die-cut style, the same 63 by 88 mm face as the boost cards. The paint can tips over a hex and a sprout rises from the splat. Palette is the card's own colour for each play, so the face wears the colour of the first splat in your hand.

Paint colours

Recipe and history

Each plant is a recipe in simulations/paint-world/alien-plants.mjs. Intent, parts, materials, decisions and the references we did not have are in studies/paint-world/assets/ (notes.json, provenance.json). Change requests make a new version; history is kept.
